question: Urban pigeons live freely in many European cities as if they were ownerless domesticated pets. With a view to keeping a lid on numbers of pigeons, many countries have banned the feeding of them. Depriving these birds, which are genetically dependent on human care, of adequate nutrition on this way causes them long periods of suffering.
This condemns not only of the parent birds, but also the chicks and flightless young pigeons to an agonising death.

Many countries still opt for this cruel course of action despite the fact that alternative measures – such as systematically replacing real eggs with fakes in supervised pigeon houses with sufficient speciesappropriate feeding or, in individual cases, the establishment of controlled, open feeding sites – have been proven effective and successful.

Experts agree that the solution is not a feeding ban, but rather the systematic, humane monitoring of pigeon lofts. Cities imposing feeding bans should be legally bound to set up pigeon lofts and controlled feeding stations throughout the area so as to comply with national animal welfare laws and Article 13 of the TFEU.

Member States should therefore allocate financial and human resources towards the running of pigeon coops. What specific measures does the Commission intend to take to persuade the Member States to abolish bans on feeding urban pigeons in favour of more animal-friendly measures?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.5.

2024) Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union requires the EU and the Member States to pay full regards to the welfare requirements of animals, when formulating and implementing EU policies and legislations, while respecting the legislative or administrative provisions and customs of the Member States relating in particular to religious rites, cultural traditions and regional heritage.

Whereas the EU has adopted animal welfare legislation during slaughter (Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009)1 and in the case of animals kept for farming purposes (Directive 98/58/EC)2, it has no competence to legislate on the welfare of animals such as city pigeons. The Rock Dove (Columba livia) is a native species to Europe that falls under the scope of protection of Directive 2009/147/EC (‘Birds Directive’).

While it is well-established that domesticated specimens have escaped from breeding installations for a long time and constitute feral populations which have sometimes interbred with wild populations, most populations of urban pigeons do not seem to descend to any significant extent from other than domestic escapees. Such populations would therefore not fall within the scope of the Birds Directive.
1 Council Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 of 24 September 2009 on the protection of animals at the time of

killing (Text with EEA relevance) OJ L 303, 18.11.2009, p. 1–30. 2 Council Directive 98/58/EC of 20 July 1998 concerning the protection of animals kept for farming purposes, OJ L 221, 8.8.1998, p. 23–27.
